body: The editor tooling of NuclearLang: one extension per editor (VS Code, Android Studio / IntelliJ, Zed) and the tools
they show (Nuclear Builder, Nuclear Connector, the chat, the devices). This folder is the index of those projects
and holds what the three extensions share. The language server is **not** here: it is
`nuclearlang/crates/nuclear-lsp`, part of [the language project](../nuclearlang/AGENTS.md). The extensions run it
as an external binary and talk to it only through LSP and the `nuclear/*` requests.

rows.title: Editor extensions — Rules
rows.summary: project.
body: - A missing feature of the server is built in `nuclearlang/crates/nuclear-lsp`, with the rules of the language
project.
- Done = `npm run compile` in `vscode/` if the client or a tool's `src/` changed, `npm test` there if Nuclear
Builder changed, `npm run theme` there if the palette changed, `jetbrains/build.sh` if the plugin or a tool's
`jetbrains/src/` changed; and the server's tests and clippy if the server changed.
- **Always release after a change** of the server, a client, the themes or the bundled dialects and type
definitions, without asking: [docs/06-runbooks/release.md](docs/06-runbooks/release.md).
- Themes and icons of the three extensions are generated by `vscode/theme/`: edit `palette.json`, `build.mjs` or
`icons.mjs`, never the generated JSON, XML or SVG.
- Framework extensions must not collide: only the base extension registers the language, the grammar and the
language server (ADR-extensions-0001).
- Nuclear Builder is for VS Code and Android Studio only (decided by the user): Zed has none.
- A tool's code and documents live in its folder under `tools/`; an extension only wires it in.

rows.title: Editor extensions — Stack
rows.summary: `zed/extension.toml`
body: - `vscode/`: TypeScript, esbuild, `vscode-languageclient`; VS Code 1.90 or newer
- `jetbrains/`: Java, compiled with `javac` against the installed IDE (no Gradle); the platform's native LSP API
- `zed/`: Rust → wasm32-wasip2, `zed_extension_api` 0.7, a tree-sitter grammar of tokens
- One version for the three (0.51.0 today): `vscode/package.json`, `jetbrains/resources/META-INF/plugin.xml`,
`zed/extension.toml`

rows.summary: A `.nuc` file is written in an editor, and what a developer does around it (run the app, debug it, call its API, give work to the agents) happens there too.
body: A `.nuc` file is written in an editor, and what a developer does around it (run the app, debug it, call its API,
give work to the agents) happens there too. The extensions bring the language to each editor and put every Nuclear
feature in one place, so working on a backend and its apps does not need several windows.

rows.title: Vision — What it does not do
rows.summary: `nuclearlang/crates/nuclear-lsp`.
body: - It is not the language server: completion, hover, diagnostics and the project rules are
`nuclearlang/crates/nuclear-lsp`.
- It does not describe a dialect: the kinds, the documentation of each word and where a project's output goes come
from the dialect and from the project card the server writes.
- No Nuclear Builder for Zed (decided by the user).
- Zed does not allow the device, `.nuc` debugging nor build on save.

rows.title: How an extension finds the language server — Dialects of the user
rows.summary: A project is checked with the dialect its manifest names.
body: A project is checked with the dialect its manifest names. `nuclear.dialectPaths` adds folders with dialects, and
`<workspace>/dialects` is always searched. Zed passes `lsp.nuclear-lsp.settings` as `{ nuclear: ... }`.

rows.title: How an extension finds the language server
rows.summary: The server is `nuclear-lsp`, built from `nuclearlang/crates/nuclear-lsp` (`cargo build --release -p nuclear-lsp` at the tree's root → `target/release/nuclear-lsp`).
body: The server is `nuclear-lsp`, built from `nuclearlang/crates/nuclear-lsp` (`cargo build --release -p nuclear-lsp` at
the tree's root → `target/release/nuclear-lsp`). Each extension runs it as an external binary. Its modules and its
behaviour are documented in [the language project](../../../nuclearlang/docs/02-architecture/language-server.md).

rows.title: How an extension finds the language server — The bundle of VS Code and JetBrains
rows.summary: `vscode/scripts/bundle-server.mjs` (`npm run server`) and `jetbrains/build.sh` build the server and copy, next to it: definitions; a dialect's `docs/` stays behind) (`nuclear-synapsis-framework/platforms/`) Both end with `nuclear-lsp --check-bundle`, which loads each bundled dialect without the…
body: `vscode/scripts/bundle-server.mjs` (`npm run server`) and `jetbrains/build.sh` build the server and copy, next to
it:
- `server/nuclear-lsp`
- `server/dialects/`: every dialect of the tree (`nuclearlang/dialects/`, each language with its frameworks and type
definitions; a dialect's `docs/` stays behind)
- `server/platforms/<platform>/platform.toml`: the contract of each platform
(`nuclear-synapsis-framework/platforms/`)
Both end with `nuclear-lsp --check-bundle`, which loads each bundled dialect without the tree and fails on any
diagnostic (N0213, for example). The server finds the dialects next to its binary; it also searches
`nuclear_dialect::install_dir()` (the installed copy).

rows.title: How an extension finds the language server — The server's life
rows.summary: stdin closes.
body: - VS Code stops the server 5 minutes after the last `.nuc` closes (`watchIdle`); the server also exits when its
stdin closes.
- The JetBrains IDE manages the server's process itself.

rows.title: How an extension finds the language server — Where each one looks, in order
rows.summary: Zed has no bundle: its server is the one `installer/install.sh` installs, which finds its dialects and type definitions in `share/nuclearlang`.
body: | Editor | Order | Code |

| VS Code | the setting `nuclear.server.path` → `server/nuclear-lsp` inside the extension → a development build beside the extension (`../target/release`, then `../target/debug`) → the `PATH` | `findServer` in `vscode/src/extension.ts` |
| Android Studio / IntelliJ | *Settings → Tools → NuclearLang* (server path) → `server/nuclear-lsp` inside the plugin → the `PATH` | `NuclearSettings.findServer` |
| Zed | `lsp.nuclear-lsp.binary.path` → the `PATH` → `~/.local/bin/nuclear-lsp` | `zed/src/lib.rs` |
Zed has no bundle: its server is the one `installer/install.sh` installs, which finds its dialects and type
definitions in `share/nuclearlang`.

rows.title: Architecture of the editor tooling — Code metrics
rows.summary: A faithful copy of the CodeMetrics extension (the user asked for the same messages): the same setting names, default costs and English texts.
body: A faithful copy of the CodeMetrics extension (the user asked for the same messages): the same setting names, default
costs and English texts. They are computed in the server; a client shows the list
(`nuclear.showCodeMetricsCodeLensInfo`) and the colors (`nuclear/codeMetrics`, or the command `nuclear.codeMetrics`
in JetBrains). For a client whose `clientInfo.name` starts with `Zed` the server answers the list with
`window/showMessage`. The editors' settings are generated from the server
(`vscode/scripts/codemetrics-settings.mjs` from `nuclear-lsp --codemetrics-defaults`): never edit
`nuclear.codemetrics.*` by hand. Credits: `vscode/THIRD-PARTY.md`.

rows.title: Architecture of the editor tooling — What a project gives the editor
rows.summary: The extensions read files; they do not assume a path, a port or a command of a dialect.
body: The extensions read files; they do not assume a path, a port or a command of a dialect.
| File of the project | Written by | Read by |

| `.nuclear/project.json` (the project card: platform, dialect, output folder, toolchain; [projects §1.1](../../../nuclearlang/docs/07-reference/projects.md)) | the server (`Project::build`) and the CLIs | the VS Code status bar, the workspace, the tools |
| `.nuclear/contract.json` (the endpoints) | the same, next to the card | Nuclear Connector |
| `.nuclear/lines.json`; `build/app/.dart_tool/nuclear_lines.json` for a mobile app | every `nuclear build` of a project; `nuclear build` | `.nuc` debugging |
| `build/<name>.code-workspace` (the tasks and the dialect's debug launch) | `nuclear build` (`tools/cli/src/framework/vscode.rs`) | run and debug in VS Code and JetBrains |
| `.nuclear/map.md` (every declaration with its kind, description and members) | the transpiler | the chat and Nuclear Builder's agents |
The JetBrains and Zed clients do not show the project card yet (the JetBrains tool windows read it only to find
the projects); the server is the same, so their diagnostics are right.

rows.title: Architecture of the editor tooling — What a project gives the editor
rows.summary: The server tells a client where a kind comes from (the language, the platform, a kind package) in hover and completion, and lists for a project only the kinds of its platform.
body: The server tells a client where a kind comes from (the language, the platform, a kind package) in hover and
completion, and lists for a project only the kinds of its platform. A file's dialect is its project's;
`nuclear.dialect` only applies to a file outside a project.

rows.title: Architecture of the editor tooling — What the three share
rows.summary: All of it lives in `vscode/` and is generated or copied for the other two (a sibling extension that is not there is skipped): VS Code, JetBrains and Zed; Zed's icon themes come from `zed/scripts/icons.mjs` over `vscode/icon-themes` (the theme).
body: All of it lives in `vscode/` and is generated or copied for the other two (a sibling extension that is not there is
skipped):
- **Themes and icons**: `vscode/theme/` (`palette.json`, `build.mjs`, `icons.mjs`) writes the Chernobyl themes of
VS Code, JetBrains and Zed; Zed's icon themes come from `zed/scripts/icons.mjs` over `vscode/icon-themes`
([the theme](../../vscode/docs/02-architecture/theme.md)).
- **The TextMate grammar**: `vscode/syntaxes/nuclear.tmLanguage.json`, also packed by `jetbrains/build.sh` (without
the `@example` patterns) and copied by the website. Zed has its own tree-sitter grammar.
- **The language configuration**: `vscode/language-configuration.json` (comments, pairs, `offSide` folding,
`onEnterRules` for ` * `); JetBrains packs it without `onEnterRules`, Zed repeats its indentation rules.
- **The code metrics settings**: generated from the server's defaults.

rows.title: Release the extensions — Steps
rows.summary: 1. Raise the version (minor for a feature, patch for a fix) in: 2. Write the change in the `CHANGELOG.md` of each extension it reaches.
body: 1. Raise the version (minor for a feature, patch for a fix) in:
- `extensions/vscode/package.json`
- `extensions/jetbrains/resources/META-INF/plugin.xml`
- `extensions/zed/extension.toml`
- the examples of each `README.md` that name a version
2. Write the change in the `CHANGELOG.md` of each extension it reaches.
3. Build:
```sh
(cd extensions/vscode && npm run package)                           # → nuclearlang-<version>.vsix
(cd extensions/jetbrains && IDE_HOME=/opt/android-studio ./build.sh) # → build/nuclearlang-<version>.zip
(cd extensions/zed && ./build.sh)                                    # builds and installs into Zed
4. Install: `installer/install.sh`. It installs the newest `.vsix` of `extensions/vscode/` (`sort -V`), rebuilds
`nuclear-builder`, and runs `extensions/zed/build.sh` when Zed is installed (`--no-zed` skips it).
5. Tell the user to quit VS Code completely (*File → Exit*: a reload does not refresh a theme) and to install the zip
in Android Studio (*Settings → Plugins → ⚙ → Install Plugin from Disk…*).

- The JetBrains plugin installed unpacked is in `~/.local/share/Google/AndroidStudio2026.2.1/nuclearlang`.
- Zed reloads the extension by itself; if not, restart Zed.

rows.summary: IDE_HOME=/opt/android-studio ./build.sh # → build/nuclearlang-<version>.zip `build.sh` needs `../vscode` beside it (the theme and the grammar), node and cargo.
body: ```sh
IDE_HOME=/opt/android-studio ./build.sh     # → build/nuclearlang-<version>.zip
`build.sh` needs `../vscode` beside it (the theme and the grammar), node and cargo. It generates the themes, builds

Install: *Settings → Plugins → ⚙ → Install Plugin from Disk…* → the zip. Then *Settings → Appearance → Theme* →

rows.title: NuclearLang for Android Studio / IntelliJ
rows.summary: The NuclearLang plugin for JetBrains IDEs: the language server (`nuclear-lsp`, from `nuclearlang/crates/nuclear-lsp`), the TextMate grammar and the Chernobyl themes of `extensions/vscode`.
body: The NuclearLang plugin for JetBrains IDEs: the language server (`nuclear-lsp`, from `nuclearlang/crates/nuclear-lsp`), the TextMate grammar and the Chernobyl themes of `extensions/vscode`.
```sh
cd extensions/jetbrains       # beside extensions/vscode, inside the NuclearLang tree
IDE_HOME=/opt/android-studio ./build.sh     # → build/nuclearlang-<version>.zip
Install: *Settings → Plugins → ⚙ → Install Plugin from Disk…* → the zip. Then: *Settings → Appearance → Theme* →
**Chernobyl** (it includes the editor's color scheme). Settings in *Settings → Tools → NuclearLang* (dialect and
server path).
A Synapsis project: *File → Open* → the project folder. The first time, the plugin adds the app (`build/app`) as
a module and offers *Reopen Project*; on reopening, the Flutter plugin gives the device picker, the `main.dart`
configuration, Run / Debug, hot reload and DevTools. Opening the project runs `nuclear build`, and **Ctrl+S on a
`.nuc`** transpiles and does a *Hot Reload* of the running app.
It uses the platform's native LSP API (`com.intellij.modules.lsp`, present in Android Studio 2026.2) and the
TextMate plugin bundled with the IDE for the grammar. It is compiled with `javac` against the installed IDE's jars:
no Gradle needed. If you only want the color scheme: *Settings → Editor → Color Scheme → ⚙ → Import* →
`extensions/jetbrains/Chernobyl.icls`.

- `Hot reload was rejected` → `Flutter.Toolbar.RestartAllAction`.

rows.title: Nuclear Connector (`nuclear-connector`)
rows.summary: The tool like Postman or Bruno inside the editor, Nuclear Connector: every endpoint of every project as a tree by platform, project and component, read from the contract the compiler writes; the contracts an app declares; OpenAPI documents of APIs that are not Nuclear; environments; and a request…
body: The tool like Postman or Bruno inside the editor, **Nuclear Connector**: every endpoint of every
project as a tree by platform, project and component, read from the contract the compiler writes; the contracts an
app declares; OpenAPI documents of APIs that are not Nuclear; environments; and a request panel. It is a tool of the
Nuclear workspace in VS Code (`Ctrl+Alt+H`) and a tool window in Android Studio / IntelliJ (`Alt+Shift+H`).

rows.title: Architecture of Nuclear Connector — A component's panel (`panel.ts`)
rows.summary: `ComponentPanel`: one webview panel per `componentKey(endpoint)`, like a Bruno folder, with an inner tab per endpoint opened from the tree.
body: `ComponentPanel`: one webview panel per `componentKey(endpoint)`, like a Bruno folder, with an inner tab per
endpoint opened from the tree. Each inner tab keeps its request and its last response:
- the method, the url with its path and query parameters, the headers, the body (with the sample);
- send: by the extension host with `fetch`, a 30 s timeout, the active environment's variables and headers;
- the response pretty-printed; *copy as curl*.
The webview posts its whole state (`tabs`, `active`) on every change and the model keeps it in `memory` by key, so
`restore(keys)` rebuilds the panels when the Connector workspace is entered again (`model.reopen` = the keys open when
it was left). The memory lives in the window, not on disk.

rows.title: Architecture of Nuclear Connector — The model (`connector.ts`)
rows.summary: `activateConnector(context)` returns the `HttpModel`.
body: `activateConnector(context)` returns the `HttpModel`.
- `findProjects` walks the workspace folders (depth 4, skipping `build`, `node_modules`…) for
`.nuclear/project.json` and reads the `contract.json` next to it. The model watches `**/.nuclear/*.json`.
- `tree()` gives the `TreeNode`s the workspace's webview draws: platform → project → *Contracts* (with ↓ update
buttons) / component → endpoint; and *OpenAPI documents* (with +) from the active environment's `openapi` list,
grouped by tag.
- `declaredContracts(root)`: the contracts an app declares in its `config.nuc`.
- `sampleOf`: a sample body from the contract's model.
- **Environments**: `<first workspace folder>/.nuclear/http.json`, else `globalStorageUri/http.json`. Its shape:
`active`, and `environments.<name>.{vars, headers, baseUrls, openapi}`. `{{var}}` is resolved by the extension
host.
Commands: `nuclear.connector.{refresh,selectEnvironment,editEnvironments,addOpenApi,open}` and
`nuclear.contracts.update (root?, name?)`, which runs `~/.local/bin/nuclear contracts update` in the project (the
output channel *Nuclear Connector*).

rows.title: The Synapsis device (`mobile-device.ts`) — The page in the panel
rows.summary: `attach` opens the extension's own CDP connection (over node's WebSocket): input lands where it is drawn.
body: `attach` opens the extension's own CDP connection (over node's WebSocket):
- **`emulate`**: metrics, touch and user agent of the preset, so Flutter behaves as on iOS or Android and every
input lands where it is drawn. The first time it is a `Page.navigate` already emulated; later a `Page.reload`,
only if the platform changes.
- **The screencast**: `Page.startScreencast` (also on `Page.loadEventFired`), jpeg 100, at `r.density` = the
physical pixels the panel shows the screen at. The webview reports `shot` = CSS width × zoom × `devicePixelRatio`
in its `size` message; `sized` sets `density = max(dpr, shot / width)`, capped at 4, and only ever raises it,
emulating again. Before the first measurement it falls back to `captureScale(p)`. So a frame matches the device's
on-screen pixels 1:1 and nothing is upscaled (a 2x cap, and even the full `dpr`, blurred phones zoomed on a HiDPI
screen).
- **Input**: `Input.dispatchTouchEvent` / `MouseEvent` / `KeyEvent`.
- It reconnects (`cdp.onclose`, 10 tries) and emulates again when a frame's size differs (every 2 s at most).
- `closeBrowser` at the end.

rows.title: Architecture of the devices — Hiding, parking, ending
rows.summary: `watchdog()` runs every `WATCH_MS` (one minute): it ends the idle devices and, with `pgrep -af` by marker, reaps the keys no app owns.
body: | What happens | Effect |
| The user closes a device's tab | the disposed panel parks its app: it goes on, hidden; the Devices pane lists it (`hidden:<key>` ids) and `revealDevice` adopts it again |
| The workspace switches tab (`Workspace.switchTabs`) | `nuclear.parkDevices` → `DevicePanel.park()`: the panels close, the apps go on with their sessions (`parked`) |

| A mobile workspace or the Devices tool is entered | `nuclear.unparkDevices` → `unpark()`, after the code is reopened: each device gets a fresh locked editor group to the right of the code (`lockDeviceGroup`), never merged into the code's group |
| ✕ of the Devices pane (`nuclear.closeDevice(id)`), the panel's ■, the end of its session | `endRunning`: the session, the CDP connection, the browser and `reap` |
| A parked app's session ends | cleaned by `endRunning` |

rows.title: NuclearLang — How it works
rows.summary: A dialect is a declarative folder (TOML + templates) loaded at run time.
body: A **dialect** is a declarative folder (TOML + templates) loaded at run time. It defines:
- the **kinds**: header words like `stateless`, `stateful`, `repository` or `controller`, which generate their
framework's structure;
- the decorators, the architecture rules and the structure of projects;
- how each construct is written in the target language.
Rust decides *what* is emitted and the dialect decides *how* it is written. To support a new framework you create a
dialect, without touching the compiler.
The **type definitions** (`defs/`, generated from the SDK, like `.d.ts`) describe each class of Dart, Flutter and
packages like bloc, dio and go_router. With them the imports are written by themselves, `@override` goes where it
belongs and the editor completes members and arguments.

rows.title: NuclearLang
rows.summary: written in Rust turns it into real code of other technologies, like Dart/Flutter or TypeScript.
body: **NuclearLang** (`.nuc`) is a minimal language, made to be written by AI agents and read by people. A transpiler
written in Rust turns it into real code of other technologies, like Dart/Flutter or TypeScript. This extension
brings the language server (`nuclear-lsp`), every dialect (flutter, fastapi, nestjs, dart, python, typescript), their type definitions and the
**Chernobyl** theme.

rows.title: NuclearLang — Philosophy
rows.summary: only if it meets the three: Principles: 1. The easiest to write.
body: **Golden rule:** performance, speed and readability. Each rule of the language and of each dialect is accepted
only if it meets the three:
- **Performance:** the generated code runs as fast as an expert's hand-written code.
- **Speed:** transpiling is immediate, because only what is needed is read.
- **Readability:** Nuclear code is minimal and is understood effortlessly.
Principles:
1. **The easiest to write.** No `;`, no `{ }` for blocks, no mandatory `return`, `new` or `this.`, no manual
`async`. Blocks are marked with a 2-space indentation.
2. **One single way to do each thing.** So an agent never hesitates between two equivalent syntaxes.
3. **Familiar before novel.** Types, `=>`, decorators and generics are written as in TypeScript.
4. **Everything is a value**, as in Elixir: `if` and `match` return, and a function's last line is its result.
5. **Clear errors before magic.** No hidden inference: every diagnostic has a code (`N0106`), a position and,
when possible, a suggested fix.
6. **The language does not change per dialect.** A dialect adds meaning, not grammar.

one target becomes a generic option or template variable any dialect can use.

- **The library is Nuclear's.** Every member of [the standard library](../../docs/07-reference/library.md) has its
template in `library.toml`; a TypeScript name (`push`, `toUpperCase`) in Nuclear code, in a reference or in an
example is a bug.
- **A framework dialect only writes the platform.** A kind, a decorator or a folder is added to the platform's
contract first, for every dialect of the platform; `frameworks/<name>/` adds how it is written in TypeScript.
- The generated code passes `tsc --strict`.
- The order of `defs` in a framework dialect decides which package gives a name two of them export: change it only
knowing which name moves.
- [`nodejs`](../nodejs/AGENTS.md) sits between this dialect and `nestjs` and is postponed by the user: do not
touch it until asked.
- `docs/07-reference/*.md` hold only final rules and real equivalences (`spec-check`, 0 problems). Never edit an
equivalence by hand: change the dialect, then `--fix` and review.
